stem: A motor lifts a $50\text{ kg}$ load through a height of $12\text{ m}$ at constant speed in $20\text{ s}$. What is the useful power output of the motor? ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$)

help.title: Useful work
help.text: At constant speed, the motor's useful work goes into raising the load. That is the gain in gravitational potential energy, $mgh$.

help.title: From energy to power
help.text: Power is the rate of doing work: $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$.

stem: A ball of mass $0.20\text{ kg}$ is dropped from a height of $2.0\text{ m}$ onto a hard floor. It rebounds to a height of $1.5\text{ m}$. Ignore air resistance and take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the ball just before it hits the floor.
markscheme: Loss of gravitational potential energy = gain in kinetic energy

help.title: Energy conservation
help.text: With no air resistance, the gravitational potential energy the ball loses as it falls becomes kinetic energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the ball's energy that is lost in the bounce.
markscheme: Energy after bounce $= mg \times 1.5$; energy lost $= mg \times 0.5$

help.title: Energy after the bounce
help.text: At the top of the rebound the ball is momentarily still, so all of its energy is potential: $mg \times 1.5$.

help.title: Fraction
help.text: Fraction lost = energy lost ÷ starting energy. Notice that $mg$ cancels, so only the heights matter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the energy that is lost.
markscheme: Transferred to internal (thermal) energy of the ball and floor and/or to sound

help.title: Energy is conserved
help.text: The 'lost' energy hasn't disappeared. During the impact, what happens to the ball and the floor, and what can you hear?

help.title: Final answer
help.text: It is transferred to **internal (thermal) energy** of the ball and floor, and to **sound**.
